inline.s: Conduct has countless aspects, but the Six Perfections are their sum. The sutras speak freely, sometimes teaching one practice:
the arousing of bodhicitta

. Or they teach two practices, called wisdom and expedient means. Or three practices: precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Or four practices, called the four abodes: first wisdom, second precepts, third giving, fourth concentration. Or five practices: giving, keeping the precepts, patience, diligence, and calm-abiding with insight. Or six practices, called the Six Perfections. The Six Perfections are giving, keeping the precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and prajna. Though the gates of practice are many, the Six Perfections embrace them all without exception.

The meaning of these Six Perfections has countless gates. Here I briefly speak of three: first, the characteristics of the Six Perfections; second, what the Six Perfections counteract; third, how the Six Perfections lead into principle.

What are their characteristics? All practices flow from bodhicitta; united, they are bodhicitta; divided, they are the Six Perfections. A mind without attachment is giving; a mind without regard to keeping or breaking is keeping the precepts; not offending a single being is patience; thought after thought unbroken is diligence; a mind that does not flow is meditation; knowing all dharmas to be empty is prajna.

What do they counteract? They counteract the six realms, so as to escape the cycle of the three worlds. The perfection of giving is established to counteract the realm of hungry ghosts; the perfection of precepts to counteract the hell realm; the perfection of patience to counteract the animal realm; the perfection of diligence to counteract the asura realm; the perfection of meditation to counteract humans and the six desire heavens; the perfection of prajna to counteract the heavens of form and formlessness.

How do they lead into principle? By following the Dharma-nature. The substance of the Dharma-nature is free of miserly greed, so the perfection of giving is established. The Dharma-nature is free of the five desires, so the perfection of precepts is established. The Dharma-nature is free of anger and vexation, so the perfection of patience is established. The Dharma-nature is free of indolence, so the perfection of diligence is established. The Dharma-nature is ever still, so the perfection of meditation is established. The Dharma-nature is free of ignorance, so the perfection of prajna is established.

The Dharma of these Six Perfections takes prajna as its master. The sutra says: “The five perfections are like the blind, and prajna is like the eye.” Giving without prajna only gains the splendor of one lifetime, and later must repay the remaining karmic debt. Keeping precepts without prajna, one is temporarily reborn in the upper desire realm and yet falls again into the mud (hell). Patience without prajna yields an upright and handsome form, but does not realize the patient endurance of cessation. Diligence without prajna wastes effort in the work of arising and ceasing, and does not reach the sea of true constancy. Meditation without prajna merely practices the meditations of the form realm and does not enter the vajra-samadhi. All good without prajna becomes only a conditioned cause, and does not accord with the unconditioned fruit.

According to the Yogacara, the bodhisattva's practice has four kinds: first, the practice of the Six Perfections; second, the practice of the factors of the path; third, the practice of the four means of gathering; fourth, the practice of spiritual powers. In sum, all take prajna as master. Though the Buddha-Dharma is divided into the Great Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, the One Vehicle, and the Three Vehicles, the Four Noble Truths already embrace them all. The cause and effect of the world are the two truths of suffering and its accumulation; the cause and effect of transcendence are the two truths of cessation and the path. Cessation is the Buddha-fruit, and the path is the bodhisattva's practice. Prajna is the substance of the path-truth, and therefore prajna is the essential practice.

[The practice of the factors of the path] is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path — altogether thirty-seven items, the important provisions for cultivating the Way. [The four means of gathering] are the means of gathering through giving, through kind speech, through beneficial conduct, and through shared activities. [The Four Noble Truths] are the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of its accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and measureless sufferings; suffering is the true reality of life. Second, “accumulation” means attracting and creating; it is the truth that explains how the suffering of life arises. The suffering of life comes from craving and attachment, which create karma, and then one experiences suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the accumulation (craving) of suffering is forever cut off without remainder, without defilement and without attachment, one no longer experiences suffering and rebirth — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to forever cut off the accumulation (craving) of suffering, that is, the way of extinguishing suffering — the eightfold noble path. Among the four noble truths, accumulation is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit. [The practice of prajna] The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms are false and unreal.” It also says: “Do not grasp at marks, and be unmoved in thusness.” It also says: “Being free of all marks, that is called all Buddhas.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “To know illusion is to be free of it, without needing expedient means; to be free of illusion is enlightenment, without any gradualism.”

blocks.text: 4. What Is Awakened: Awakening to Dependent Origination

inline.s: Whether studying the teachings or meditating in Chan, all seek great and thorough enlightenment. The state of thorough awakening is the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen. The student single-mindedly seeks awakening — what dharma is it, in the end, that is awakened? I reply: awakening to dharmas that arise from conditions. What are dharmas arising from conditions? They are dharmas produced by causes and conditions. All dharmas arise when conditions gather and cease when conditions disperse; not existing yet seeming to exist, their illusory forms are unreal; what exists is not existing, and in substance they are emptiness.
[The true characteristic of dharmas] The true state of all dharmas. The Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter on Reciting the Buddha's Name, the Buddha says: “What is called the true characteristic of dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything existing.” The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms are false and unreal.”

The reply: since the marks of dependent origination are already false and unreal, how can awakening to marks be the summit of achievement? The reply: if one's seeing of the nature is not true, one cannot understand the marks; if one's seeing of the nature is true, then one can clearly see that the vast array of all phenomena are all produced by causes and conditions upon one's own nature, which is called wondrous existence. Therefore the essential point of studying the Dharma is to understand that dependent origination is empty of self-nature. If one sees the nature of conditions, one is free from the bonds of conditions. (The nature of conditions means the nature of dependent origination, which is the Buddha-nature. The twelve links of dependent origination are the marks of the cycle of rebirth; the Buddha-nature is the nature of that cycle, and seeing the Buddha-nature instantly cuts off the cycle. The bonds of conditions are the bonds of the cycle of the twelve links of dependent origination.) Therefore, realizing the nature is to understand dependent origination, and to understand dependent origination is to realize the true nature — these are one matter.

Students of the Great Vehicle are taught to contemplate dependent origination from the very outset, in order to prepare the proper cause for future awakening. What does this mean? The Buddha-Dharma takes emptiness as its master, and its teaching of emptiness takes causes and conditions as its tenet; causes and conditions are the meaning of dependent origination (“dependent arising” means dependent origination). Ordinary people do not believe it, followers of non-Buddhist paths do not know it, and the Lesser Vehicle's provisional teachings, though they know of it, do not know it thoroughly; only the great bodhisattvas who study the Buddha Vehicle must focus on it the most. Why? Because when the Buddha speaks of the mind-ground, he speaks of the two emptinesses. Without the meaning of dependent origination, the two emptinesses cannot be established.

The discriminating mind of people creates good and evil karma, and so there is rising and sinking, but the true mind is originally unmoving. The discriminating mind is a burden, and one suffers the cycle of rebirth in vain. One should know that delusion, karma, and suffering are all produced by causes and conditions; dependent origination is empty of self-nature, and so it is called the emptiness of persons. The sense-faculties and sense-objects are likewise produced by causes and conditions; faculties and objects have no self-nature, all is empty, and so it is called the emptiness of dharmas. Without the meaning of dependent origination, persons and dharmas would both be real, and the true mind would not manifest. With the meaning of dependent origination, persons and dharmas are both empty, the true mind manifests, and one attains the fundamental dharma-body, which is the Buddha-fruit. The dharma-body is like empty space, so it is called true emptiness. Within the body of true emptiness, all the lands as numerous as dust in the ten directions are all manifest. Hence the Nirvana Sutra says: “The Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the ultimate truth; the emptiness of the ultimate truth is itself wisdom.” And the Sandhinirmocana Sutra says: “If one does not understand the dharmas without marks, the defiled dharmas with marks cannot be cut off; and because the defiled dharmas with marks are not cut off, one destroys the realization of the subtle pure dharmas with marks.” If one can awaken to dependent origination, one realizes the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen, which is great and thorough enlightenment. Students of the Great Vehicle should practice thus — strive on, strive on!

[Emptiness] In describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “nonexistence,” there is another situation, that of illusory appearance — like things in a dream, having form but no real substance, not truly existing — and the concept “emptiness” is used to describe it. The Vimalakirti Sutra

Chapter on the Disciples, the third, says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything existing; this is the meaning of emptiness.” In this sentence, “all dharmas” speaks of the existence of marks, and “ultimately without anything existing” speaks of real nonexistence; this situation of having marks yet being really nonexistent (illusion) is called emptiness.

blocks.text: 1. What Is Meant by Arousing the Mind

inline.s: To arouse bodhicitta, whose full form is “to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi,” is also called simply “arousing the mind.” Bodhicitta is the pure mind of self-nature. This pure mind of self-nature is equal in sentient beings and Buddhas, possessed by everyone, neither increasing nor decreasing. “Arousing” means to initiate and to develop. To arouse bodhicitta is to initiate and develop this pure mind of self-nature. The initial mind is only the initiating; seeing the nature is called the developing. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse bodhicitta is to contemplate this pure mind of self-nature. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: “What is bodhi? It is to know one's own mind as it truly is.”
[Bodhi] is translated into Chinese as “awakening.”
Question: What is meant by the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: The pure mind of self-nature is our true mind. Because this mind has the nature of awakening, it is called the Buddha-nature. Because it is the root of all dharmas, it is called the dharma-body. Because it never changes, it is called thusness. Because its nature is not false, it is called the true characteristic. Because it knows all things, it is called bodhi. Because it is still and unmoving, it is called nirvana. Because it is the nature of all dharmas, it is called the Dharma-nature. All these various names are different names for our true mind. Everyone originally possesses it, everyone is fully endowed with it; it is near, within the mind, and there is no need to seek it far away. To become a Buddha or a patriarch is this one mind; false thoughts rely on it to form the three worlds, and it is the basis of the world's establishment and the source of life's dependent origination. Sentient beings, not knowing this, from time without beginning have never contemplated it, and in vain create the cycle of rebirth, sinking in birth and death.
Question: Why contemplate the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: As said above, to arouse bodhicitta is to initiate and develop the pure mind of self-nature. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse bodhicitta is to contemplate this pure mind of self-nature. The Buddha-Dharma teaches people to turn back and contemplate within, which is to enter the Buddha-nature, to enter the dharma-body, to enter thusness, to enter the true characteristic, to enter nirvana, to enter the Dharma-nature, and to enter the Dharma-realm. It instantly cuts off the cycle of rebirth and quickly escapes birth and death. Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma is the mind, and the root of the practice is contemplation. The Sutra of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle says: “Within the three worlds, the mind is master; one who can contemplate the mind is ultimately liberated, and one who cannot is forever in bondage.” The Nirvana Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the highest concentration.”
Question: To arouse bodhicitta is to arouse the mind of compassion and vows; why is it said to be contemplating the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: Arousing bodhicitta has two kinds: first, the mundane; and second, the ultimate. To arouse the mind of compassion and vows is a conditioned dharma, called the mundane. To contemplate the pure mind of self-nature is an unconditioned dharma, called the ultimate. The mundane cannot encompass the ultimate, but the ultimate can encompass the mundane.
Question: Great compassion and great vows are essential practices of the Buddha-Dharma; why are they set aside here?

I reply: It is not that they are set aside. For one who has not seen the nature, compassion and vows are very narrow; only upon seeing the nature can they become vast; therefore seeing the nature is most urgent. What is called compassion and vows is but seeking the Buddha-way above and transforming sentient beings below. Now, to seek to see the nature is originally in order to become a Buddha and benefit sentient beings, which is itself great compassion and great vows — why need one arouse them again?
Question: Does this kind of arousing the mind have other names?

Answer: Yes. When contemplating, not dwelling on external objects, it is called the practice of no-thought. When the one mind is unmoving, it is called the practice of not-moving. When the mind has no object of support, it is called the practice of no-marks. When the mind does not abide in objects, it is called the practice of no-abiding. When one contemplates with prajna (not giving rise to a discriminating mind while contemplating), it is called the practice of prajna. In short, to constantly cultivate this practice is to be free of discrimination, free of subject and object, which is to be free of mind, thought, and consciousness; once mind, thought, and consciousness are free, the true mind naturally manifests. Such is the function of arousing the mind — thus, and thus.

[Subject and object] The active dharma is called “subject,” and the passive dharma is called “object.” For example, in the six faculties confronting the six objects, the six faculties are the active perceiving and the six objects are the perceived. Here “subject and object” refers to the contemplator and the contemplated. [Mind, thought, and consciousness] “Mind” refers to the eighth consciousness (alaya-vijnana), “thought” refers to the seventh consciousness (manas), and “consciousness” refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness).
Question: What does “contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” mean?

Answer: “Contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” means that the key to Chan contemplation is to be free of mind, thought, and consciousness; once the subtle thoughts come to rest, self-nature reveals itself in its original state, which is to see the mind and realize the nature.

To attain seeing the mind and realizing the nature, there are three steps: first, the coarse thoughts come to rest (ten thousand thoughts return to one); second, the fine thoughts come to rest (the one thought returns to nothing); third, the subtle thoughts come to rest (both subject and object vanish, and faculties and objects are entirely released). When the subtle thoughts come to rest, self-nature is restored from the state of habitual nature to the state of original nature; at this time one thoroughly sees the original nature, which is what is commonly called seeing the mind and realizing the nature. Therefore “contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” means that Chan contemplation should pass, through non-discrimination and freedom from subject and object, to the point where “both subject and object vanish and faculties and objects are entirely released,” in order to thoroughly see the original nature.

[Coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts] Mind-thoughts have three kinds: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, delusive thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is a fine thought. Usually, when both coarse and fine thoughts are stilled, it is called no-thought; this is the no-thought generally spoken of. Further, if subtle thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. [Subtle thoughts] The subtle arising and ceasing flow of the discriminating mind is the characteristic of the alaya-vijnana.
Question: What is the original nature?

Answer: Self-nature has these two states, delusion and awakening. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When self-nature is deluded, that is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened, that is a Buddha.” Self-nature awakened is the original state of self-nature, called the original nature. To see the nature is to see the original nature. When self-nature gives rise to thoughts and moves, it is in the state of delusion, called the habitual nature; this is the deep-rooted habitual state that self-nature has formed from time without beginning, by producing thoughts and relying on objects (the seeds of ignorance, which by long standing have become a nature). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Self-nature contains all dharmas; this is called the store consciousness. If it gives rise to thinking, that is the transforming consciousness.” In this passage the Sixth Patriarch gives an extremely important instruction on self-nature: when self-nature is deluded (gives rise to thinking), it transforms from the state of original nature into the state of habitual nature. And practice is to restore self-nature from the state of habitual nature to the state of original nature, and so one goes from being a sentient being to becoming a Buddha.
Question: Why arouse bodhicitta?

Answer: In order to see the mind and realize the nature. Hence it is said: one who arouses the mind arouses the mind that seeks to see the nature. To study Buddhism without seeking to see the nature is to be a follower of non-Buddhist paths; only one who resolves to see the nature is a child of the Buddha. If one sees the mind and realizes the nature, afflictions are cut off of themselves without being cut off; karmic obstructions are removed of themselves without being removed; all sufferings are extinguished of themselves without being extinguished; and though one does not speak of making offerings to the Three Jewels, one has already made offerings to the Three Jewels of one's own mind; though one gives not a single coin, one's giving surpasses the seven treasures; though one does not recite mantras, one obtains the seal of the mantras; though one does not recite the sutras, the twelve divisions of scripture are all penetrated. Because one proceeds from the root, the fruit is thus great and the merit thus high.
Question: How is it that contemplating the mind attains seeing the nature?

Answer: The ancients said: “If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no source.” Because the Buddha-Dharma all rests on the pure mind; only by turning back and contemplating within can one draw forth the Buddha-nature, and then all the gates of samadhi, all the gates of dharani, all the gates of liberation, and all the gates of spiritual power manifest at once. Therefore know that the mind is the source of the wondrous Dharma; if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn forth? Thus contemplating the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma, which no other practice can match. Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra says: “At the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment.” This means that one's own mind is the Buddha; seeing one's own true Buddha, one attains right enlightenment. The Treatise on the Arousing of Bodhicitta says: “If a person seeks the Buddha's wisdom and penetrates bodhicitta, this body born of parents will quickly attain the stage of great enlightenment.” The people of today wish to become Buddhas, yet they race their minds outward seeking — alas! Without ever arousing the mind, they cultivate sundry contemplations and practices, gaining only the fruit of rebirth in the heavens, and cannot escape the cycle of rebirth.
Question: What is the relationship between arousing bodhicitta and the other contemplative practices?

Answer: Arousing bodhicitta is the general characteristic; the other contemplative practices are the particular characteristics. The particular must rely on the general, and the general can encompass the particular. The Nirvana Sutra says: “Though one believes the particular characteristics, if one does not believe the characteristic of the one undifferentiated body (that is, bodhicitta), it is called incomplete faith. Because faith is incomplete, all the precepts are also incomplete, and all extensive learning is also incomplete.” The ancients said: “Without bodhicitta, even the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts are not accomplished, because one does not know the root of the Buddha-Dharma.” Such is its importance. The people of today learn a bellyful of Buddha-Dharma, yet are utterly confused here — why?

blocks.text: 3. The Merit of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: The merit of arousing the mind cannot be fully spoken of; it pervades the many sutras, and is extensively set forth in the Avatamsaka, the Yogacara, and the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom. Here I cite a few items below:
1. The Benefits of Taking Birth

Having aroused this mind, one obtains four benefits: (1) The seed is supreme, because bodhicitta is the seed. (2) The mother that gives birth is supreme, because prajna-paramita is the mother that gives birth. (3) The womb is supreme, because the bliss of great meditation is the womb. (4) The wet-nurse is supreme, because great compassion nourishing is the wet-nurse.
2. The Merit of Leaving Home

A layman cannot obtain the merit of leaving home; but if a layman arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, it is equal to leaving home, and he too can obtain this merit. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “Do you arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this is to leave home, and this is to be fully endowed.” (The passage reads: “Then Vimalakirti said to the sons of the elders: You should together leave home within the true Dharma. Why? Because a Buddha's appearance in the world is hard to encounter! The sons of the elders said: Layman, we have heard the Buddha say that without the parents' permission one cannot leave home. Vimalakirti said: Indeed! Do you arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this is to leave home, and this is to be fully endowed.”)
[Not permitted] Not allowed.
3. Being Fully Endowed with the Buddha-Dharma

The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “To arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, everything is fully endowed.” The Vibhasa Treatise says: “This Dharma-gate is the mother of the Buddhas, the father of the Buddhas, the eye of the Buddhas, the mother of the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen, the mother of great compassion and great mercy; constantly cultivate it, and the merit is measureless and boundless.” The Great Prajna Sutra says: “It is like shooting an arrow at an object — sometimes it hits, sometimes it misses; but shooting an arrow at the ground, there is none that does not hit.” One who arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and becomes a Buddha is like shooting an arrow at the ground — there is none that does not succeed.
4. Entering the Eons and Transcending the Eons

Worldly people often resent that becoming a Buddha takes three great asamkhya eons, and that the time is too far. They do not know that those who cultivate sundry contemplative practices are still outside the three great asamkhya eons. Today, having aroused the mind, one who has not entered the eons enters them, and one who has already entered them can transcend them.
5. The Buddhas' Prediction and the Buddhas' Blessing

At the first arousing of the mind, the Buddhas give their prediction; this is clearly stated in many sutras, such as the Sutra of the Birth of Bodhi, the Sutra of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle, the Sutra of the Questions of the Youth, and most extensively in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the Buddhas' blessing, the Lankavatara Sutra says: “In all the lands of the ten directions, all the immeasurable Buddhas extend their hands of light and stroke the crown of this person's head.” Thus the Buddhas constantly bless such a practitioner.
6. Being Able to Transform the Female Body
In the canon there is the Sutra of Transforming the Female Body. When the Buddha spoke of bodhicitta, eight hundred laywomen were transformed into male bodies.
7. Rebirth in the Highest Grade

Worldly people recite the Buddha's name without knowing to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; even if they attain rebirth, they only attain the middle or lower grades. If, while reciting the Buddha's name, they also arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then they may hope for rebirth in the highest grade. The Contemplation Sutra says: not knowing the ultimate truth, one cannot attain rebirth in the highest grade. The ultimate truth is bodhicitta. There are many other sutras; I will not cite them all here.
8. Being Free of Disasters and Calamities

The Vibhasa Treatise says: “Calamity, fire, officialdom, thieves, enmity, poison, dragons, wild beasts, and massed illness — that they should afflict this person is without any likelihood. For this person is constantly guarded, thought of, and praised by the eight classes of devas and nagas and by all the Buddhas.” This treatise briefly lists nine kinds of disasters and calamities: first, the calamity of eons; second, the calamity of fire; third, official troubles; fourth, the calamity of thieves; fifth, enmity; sixth, poison and harm; seventh, the calamity of dragons; eighth, vicious beasts; ninth, illness. In fact, all disasters are entirely eliminated. The full account is as in the Avatamsaka and the Yogacara-bhumi Treatise.
9. The Essential Path to Buddhahood

The Bhadrakalpa Sutra says: “The Tathagata Star King, formerly a cowherd, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Sound-Giving. The Tathagata Name-Accomplished, formerly a weaver, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Lightning-Light. The Tathagata Bright-Flame, formerly a city-guardian, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Boundless-Light. The Tathagata Hard-to-Vanquish, formerly a woodcutter, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Firm-Stepping. The Tathagata Merit-Banner, formerly a water-drawer, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Wondrous-Name. The Tathagata Power-Army, formerly a physician, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Great-Parable.” This passage illustrates the following three points: First, lowly origins: cowherds, weavers, and such are not from high families, so arousing bodhicitta is not restricted by one's position or family. Second, attaining the fruit: these six all attained the fruit of the Tathagata, showing that arousing bodhicitta is not in vain. Third, the essential path: they attained the Buddha-fruit not by the merit of other contemplative practices but by the merit of arousing bodhicitta; therefore arousing bodhicitta is the essential path to Buddhahood.
Question: Arousing bodhicitta is certainly about quickly becoming a Buddha; if one does not succeed in this life, is there any fruit?

I reply: There is. From the arousing of bodhicitta up to the attainment of Buddhahood, the intermediate births are called in the Yogacara treatises “the successively superior births,” meaning that in life after life the benefits double and increase. The Sutra of the Birth of Bodhi says: if one seeks riches and honor, or to become a king of the heavens, one can obtain it as one wishes. How can one say there is no fruit? Moreover, if one truly arouses bodhicitta, from the stage of the ten faiths onward one becomes thirteen kinds of Dharma-teachers, that is, thirteen kinds of kings among humans and gods. This meaning is seen in the Sutra of the Benevolent King and the Sutra of the Garland of Jewels. The first item above, “the benefits of taking birth,” sums up its fruit, which the treatises call obtaining the four holy wheels.
Question: How does one arouse bodhicitta?

Answer: The Sutra of Manjusri's Questions says: “Not arousing is the arousing of bodhicitta.” What does “not arousing” mean? It means not arousing any mind that seeks benefit, or any mind of compassion and vows that has conditions. For when one arouses the mind, one must set aside all external conditions and be free of thoughts, pure and clean. To give rise to thoughts and set the mind moving is to go against the substance of the Dharma, hence “not arousing.” Then why is it also called “arousing”? Because when thought after thought is all still, and self-nature is perfectly fused, pervading without limit — that is arousing the mind. Wisdom functions within, not without, and so “not arousing” is “arousing.” The Flower-Hand Sutra says: “Contemplate this mind; thought after thought it arises and ceases, illusory and without anything existing, yet it obtains great fruit-reward.” Layman Pang said: “Only see the place of arising and ceasing; this is thusness.” Savor these words well.

There are three further essential points: First, when arousing the mind, one should know there is no agent that arouses — this destroys attachment to self. Second, there is no realm in which it is aroused. Third, there is no expedient means by which it is aroused. These two destroy attachment to dharmas. In sum, the aim is ultimately emptiness, nothing existing, nothing attained.

Moreover, when arousing the mind, if any wondrous states or even small spiritual powers appear, one should immediately abandon them, because this is a dharma without marks. All sundry practices and all sundry contemplations must not be mixed in with this cultivation.

blocks.text: 5. The Ritual of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: The ritual of arousing bodhicitta:

The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Noble Teachings says: “Standing respectfully before the wise one, rouse the exalted intention and make this vow: I, disciple So-and-so, from today onward, arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Because I wish to benefit all sentient beings, whatever I cultivate, the Six Perfections and so forth, are all for the sake of realizing anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. I now walk the same path as the great bodhisattva-mahasattvas; may the venerable one vouch for it.” Saying this three times accords with the ritual.

In the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan it says: You cultivate no-thought, yet your discriminating mind is great; how can you accord with prajna? I think of how earnestly you seek the Dharma; now I should teach you to arouse the ultimate bodhicitta (urging the arousal of the true mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi):
A. Four matters to examine beforehand. (Not for use while in sitting meditation; one should know them beforehand.)
One, for what purpose? (If it is for the sake of gaining benefit, the cause is not upright; one should seek to see the mind and realize the nature.)
Two, wash away old views. (One should wash away old views and old hearing until thoroughly clean.)
Three, with what mind? (One should be free of the mind of perception, that is, free of mind, thought, and consciousness, and not employ the mind.)
Four, what practice? (Not mixing in the marks of dharmas, solely the one method of contemplating the mind and guarding the mind unmoving.)
B. The method of proper practice. (This method is based on the four lines transmitted by Master Bodhidharma. Those with true faith may all study it; those without faith should not.)
One, harmonize all external conditions to rest. (Cast away the affairs of faculties and objects until thoroughly clean.)
Two, within, the mind has no panting. (“Panting” means movement; it says the mind does not move.)
Three, the mind is like a wall. (It says discrimination does not arise, and one is free of subject and object.)
Four, one may enter the Way. (This line is the fruit; the effort is only in the three lines above.)

Every day seated in full lotus, contemplate the mind according to the three lines. If a mind-thought arises, neither suppress it nor follow it; one should contemplate that delusive thoughts have no self-nature, and that their substance is empty, and the mind will naturally become still. When delusive thoughts cease, the spring of the mind is empty and still, prajna accords, and the true nature first manifests. This method is the practice of no-thought, the practice of no-abiding, the practice of not-moving, which is the samadhi of thusness; it breathes through the same nostril as the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, and instantly realizes in a single thought. (During contemplation one should not let states appear; this is most important. The number of sittings and their length may be as one pleases.)
C. The ceremony of receiving the Dharma.

One must bathe, then bow to the Buddha and say: “Disciple So-and-so, today from such-and-such a worthy one, I study arousing bodhicitta; I believe and rejoice, and will practice it my whole life, vowing never to forget.” Saying this three times, do three prostrations. Afterwards, simply practice, and no further declaration is needed. From then on, one may not be negligent for a single day.
[From then on, one may not be negligent for a single day.] Most important! Most important!

Recitation may be reduced; the Diamond Sutra may be recited — who says all sutras must be recited every day? Now, merely by arousing bodhicitta one directly enters the realm of the sages; why be greedy for more?

blocks.text: 6. The Three Essentials of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: Surveying the bodhisattva-pitaka, about three-tenths of it speaks of the meaning of arousing the mind. In the chapters and commentaries of the great masters it is explained in detail item by item, and the categories of meaning are especially many. Here I briefly speak thus. Finally there are three essential points: First, one must believe that one's own mind is the Buddha; second, one must have a good spiritual friend to teach; third, one must be willing to diligently contemplate the mind. Possessing these three essentials, there is no one who does not become a Buddha. Even a moment's cultivation plants the Buddha-seed. Its supreme merit cannot be compared with the ordinary recitation of sutras, reciting the Buddha's name, reciting mantras, and other contemplative practices.

Ordinarily one should often think over the principle of mind-only, that one's own mind is the Buddha, the meaning of the two emptinesses, and that all dharmas have no self-nature, as a preparation. Nurturing and self-examination are especially not to be neglected. One should know that worldly affairs are like dreams and illusions, and life is like the morning dew; in a moment it is all impermanent, and everything is in vain. If one can stir up the thought of indifference and the thought of renunciation, one most easily accords. To cultivate with a single thought for ten thousand years — that is it.
The Ratnakuta Sutra verse says
Were one to build stupas, as many as the sands of the Ganges,
Yet it would not compare with a single moment of thinking on this matter.
Though one pass through all future eons, visiting all Buddha-lands,
Without seeking this wondrous Dharma, one can never attain bodhi.
[Thinking on this matter] Contemplating the nature of the mind (contemplating the mind). The original note says: “‘Thinking’ means contemplation, and ‘this matter’ means the nature of the mind.”
The Avatamsaka Sutra verse says:
A child of the Buddha, having first aroused such a wondrous jewel-mind,
Then transcends the stage of the ordinary man and enters where the Buddha walks,
Born in the Tathagata's family, his lineage without flaw,
Equal with the Buddha, he will surely attain supreme enlightenment.

The above is roughly the meaning the Master often taught. If one can give rise to a single thought of faith, a moment's cultivation already has measureless merit; how much more so diligent and focused cultivation, whose recompense is beyond thought. May all who study, and who are fortunate enough to hear this, each treasure it and encourage themselves.
Question: I suspect that the method of arousing the mind is too high, suited to the highest faculties and not to the middling and low.
[Servant] A humble term for “I.”

Answer: It is not high. If one does not arouse the mind, one is not genuine. The Avatamsaka says: it is like taking medicine — if the medicine does not match the illness, one may keep changing it; only the single flavor of water cannot be changed. Water is a metaphor for bodhicitta. The later masters speak of the method of reciting the Buddha's name and do not speak of arousing the mind — first, because the ignorant do not know it, and second, because their method is not complete. The three Pure Land sutras — the Larger Amitabha (referring to the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha) and the Contemplation Sutra (the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha) — both have passages on arousing the mind; it is wrong to say that the Smaller Amitabha (referring to the Amitabha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha) has none. This sutra (the Amitabha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha) has the words “non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi”; if one had not first aroused the mind, with respect to what would one speak of non-retrogression? This meaning has never been explained by anyone; think it over and it becomes clear by itself.
Question: I suspect that one who recites the Buddha's name while also cultivating the arousal of the mind will be mixed and impure.

Answer: It is not mixed. Does not reciting the Buddha's name seek single-minded concentration? (For one who has never contemplated the mind, how can he know single-minded concentration?) The one method of arousing the mind directly enters the state of single mind; how can it be said to be mixed? Moreover, when we recite the Buddha's name from morning to night, can our three karmas of body, speech, and mind be never apart from the Buddha? In dealing with affairs and meeting people, can we be never apart from the Buddha for even an instant? If one says, not yet — we are apart from the Buddha for much of the time. Then in this separation one does not complain of the mixture, yet in a single arousal of the mind one alone complains of the mixture — is that acceptable? For a student of the Dharma to refuse to arouse the mind, I fear there is no such principle.
